scenes.name: Nueva psicodelia y big music: Echo & the Bunnymen y U2
scenes.book: Postpunk. Romper todo y empezar de nuevo
scenes.author: Simon Reynolds
scenes.desc: En lugar de descender a lo oscuro, elevarse hacia la luz. Liverpool, que no tuvo punk clásico ni postpunk experimental, quería que la música fuera «una fiesta» (Bill Drummond, Zoo): el club Eric's, las bandas fantasma (The Crucial Three, Big in Japan), Wah! Heat, The Teardrop Explodes de Julian Cope. Echo & the Bunnymen, con el minimalismo aprendido de Television y la voz de Ian McCulloch, graban Crocodiles y Heaven Up Here, respuesta luminosa a Closer, y heredan el público huérfano de Joy Division; Ocean Rain los vuelve estrellas pop. U2, «punk positivo» cristiano y pacifista, guitarra de The Edge como sintetizador, quiere ocupar el lugar de Curtis: War (1983), «Sunday Bloody Sunday» en MTV, The Unforgettable Fire con Eno. Alrededor, la «big music» celta de Simple Minds, The Waterboys, Big Country y la neopsicodelia de The Blue Orchids.

podcast.title: Collaboration with Johnny Marr (1993)
podcast.body: In 1993, while estranged from Echo and the Bunnyman, Ian McCulloch collaborated with ex-Smiths guitarist Johnny Marr, writing at least an album's worth of material. This project generated significant excitement in the British music press, especially when Echo guitarist Will Sargent joined them. "In 1993, Ian McCulloch was still estranged from Echo and the Bunnyman, and he was looking to get back into the game. At the same time, ex-Smith's guitarist, Johnny Marr, wanted to do something new. They wrote at least an album's worth of material together, and the British music press went nuts, speculating over the possibilities."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Alleged Theft of Master Tapes
podcast.body: The finished album from Ian McCulloch's collaboration with Johnny Marr and Will Sargent was never released, with legend stating that the master tapes were stolen from a courier truck in a hold-up, and no backups existed. This led to the album being lost, although its authenticity and the theft story itself have been questioned. "According to legend, the master tapes were sent to the record company after everything had been completed. But somewhere along the line, they were stolen from the career truck in a hold-up. There were no backups, and the album was lost."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Theories Behind Unreleased Album
podcast.body: Two main theories exist regarding the unreleased Ian McCulloch/Johnny Marr album. One suggests the theft story was fabricated by Ian to facilitate his return to Echo and the Bunnyman without interference from the collaboration. Another theory proposes the music was of poor quality due to frequent arguments between Ian and Johnny, indicating the album might never have been truly completed. "The theory is that Ian and Johnny made up the story because Ian wanted to get back with the Bunnieman, and this project would have ruined everything. Another theory is that the music was crap because Ian and Johnny were arguing so much that an album never really was completed."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Collaboration with Ian McCulloch (1993)
xref.body: In 1993, former Smiths guitarist Johnny Marr sought new creative endeavors and collaborated with Ian McCulloch, who was then estranged from Echo and the Bunnyman. Together, they wrote enough material for an album, generating considerable buzz in the British music press, a project that later included Will Sargent but ultimately went unreleased. "At the same time, ex-Smith's guitarist, Johnny Marr, wanted to do something new. They wrote at least an album's worth of material together, and the British music press went nuts, speculating over the possibilities."

xref.title: Alleged Theft of Master Tapes
xref.body: The collaboration album between Johnny Marr and Ian McCulloch was reportedly stolen from a courier truck, with no backups, leading to its loss. This alleged theft is the stated reason for the album's unreleased status, though theories suggest the story might have been fabricated or the music was incomplete. "According to legend, the master tapes were sent to the record company after everything had been completed. But somewhere along the line, they were stolen from the career truck in a hold-up. There were no backups, and the album was lost."

xref.title: Involvement in McCulloch-Marr Project
xref.body: Echo guitarist Will Sargent was brought in to assist on the collaboration project between Ian McCulloch and Johnny Marr, further exciting the British music press. He later joined McCulloch in the band Electra Fiction, which re-recorded some songs from the lost album. "Then Echo guitarist Will Sargent was brought into help. That got them even more excited."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Re-recording of Lost Album Tracks
xref.body: Two songs from the unreleased collaboration album between Ian McCulloch and Johnny Marr were re-recorded for the band Electra Fiction, which featured McCulloch and Echo guitarist Will Sargent. This provided a partial glimpse into the material that was reportedly stolen. "Well, not entirely. Two songs were re-recorded for a band called Electra Fiction, which featured Ian and Will."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Theories Behind Unreleased Album
xref.body: The unreleased collaboration album between Johnny Marr and Ian McCulloch is surrounded by speculation. One theory posits that the theft story was concocted to allow Ian McCulloch to rejoin Echo and the Bunnyman without complications. Another suggests the album was never truly completed due to creative conflicts and poor quality resulting from frequent arguments between Marr and McCulloch. "The theory is that Ian and Johnny made up the story because Ian wanted to get back with the Bunnieman, and this project would have ruined everything. Another theory is that the music was crap because Ian and Johnny were arguing so much that an album never really was completed."

xref.title: Vocals on World Cup Theme Song
xref.body: A song originally from the unreleased collaboration between Ian McCulloch and Johnny Marr ended up being used as a World Cup theme song, featuring vocals from The Spice Girls. This unexpected use of the track provided a different outlet for some of the material from the reportedly stolen album. "And another ended up as a World Cup theme song with vocals from The Spice Girls."
